newsitem.title: USA: Is inflation a threat? Here's what to do.
newsitem.headline: Is inflation a threat? Here's what to do.

text.p: A year ago, investors in the bond market were worried about inflation. They've recently grown worried again. Does that mean that you should be too?
While inflation affects everyone, bond market investors are especially watchful for signs of it since it erodes the returns on their long-term investments.

While long-term bond rates touched 7 percent last week after hitting 7.17 percent in April -- a sign bond investors are concerned about a pickup in inflation -- experts are divided over whether rapid economic growth will lead to higher inflation.
So far there have been scant signs of a pickup in prices and wages.
But it pays to be prepared, financial planning experts said. Even if inflation is running at only 3 percent a year, something that costs $1,000 today will cost $1,344 a decade from now.

"Inflation is always looming in the background. We should always be prepared for it," said Don Silver, a Los Angeles estate planning attorney. "A generation ago inflation was quite bad, and people tend to forget that."
While virtually no one expects interest rates to jump near 20 percent, as they did in the late 1970s, taking a few modest steps now can help protect your assets from inflation.

Precious metals and real estate have been traditional inflation hedges. But in today's environment, you're probably better off with real estate and fixed-income investments, rather than precious metals, several experts said.
"Gold is out," said Jonathan Pond, a Watertown, Mass., financial planner and investment adviser. "Real estate has, is and always will be the best way for people of average means to create wealth."
It also can be a good hedge against inflation. Prices have recovered some ground in recent years but are still below the inflation-driven peak reached in the late 1980s in many areas.

There are several ways to invest in real estate. Buying property directly is one but that often means being a landlord. Alternatives include real estate funds, investment trusts and other "indirect" investments.

"We're due for a small pickup in inflation, not a big one, so it's wise to protect yourself," said Jack Everett, a financial planner from Roseville, Calif., near Sacramento. "One of the best areas to look at is real estate."
Everett does not recommend real estate investment trusts, which are like real estate mutual funds, because they often closely track the stock market and so do not provide real diversity.

Rather, he suggests investing in partnerships open to outside investors. He recommended Wells Real Estate Funds (800 448-1010, minimum investment $1,000), which seeks 10 percent to 15 percent returns on 10- to 15-year investments.

The funds invest in suburban office buildings, shopping malls and similar assets. The partnership units are registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission but the investments are not guaranteed. They are also not very liquid and selling early can mean taking a big loss.

Another company is CNL Investment Co., an Orlando concern that buys fast food restaurant real estate and offers trust and partnership investments (407 422-1574, minimum investment $2,500; $1,000 for individual retirement accounts).
Everett recommended putting 15 percent of assets in real estate, not counting your home, as an inflation hedge, up from the 10 percent he had suggested previously.
Buying property directly is another way to go but don't overpay -- the single biggest mistake most investors make.
"Don't fall in love with it," said Pond, adding that a good rule of thumb is not to pay more than seven times the actual gross annual rental the property will generate.
Bonds are also a good inflation hedge, with shorter maturities less likely to get hurt if inflation surges.
Pond said three-year and five-year U.S. Treasury bonds were attractive, yielding about 6.33 percent and 6.48 percent, respectively.
Zero-coupon Treasury bonds were another good hedge, he said. You buy the bond at a discount and receive interest at the end of the bond's life when you get the full face value.
For example, a 16-year zero-coupon bond that costs about $3,300 now will pay $10,000 in May 2013, an effective annual yield of about 7.07 percent.
"There are times in life that 7 percent sure is better than 25 percent maybe," Pond said, noting stock prices seem high. "You're getting a riskless return of 7 percent."
Zero-coupons would be good for 10 to 20 percent of a portfolio, said Pond, who hosts "Your Financial Future" on public television stations across the country.

One downside of zero-coupon bonds: the government will tax the imputed interest each year even though you don't get the funds until maturity. One way around it: put the zeros in an IRA or other retirement account where income is tax-deferred.
